steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on ClassInSight, a tool that visualizes classroom discussion data for personalized teacher professional development. Cover why teachers lack good feedback, the limits of current options, prior work on discussion analytics, our research questions and long-term deployment with teachers, and our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Teaching is constantly changing; feedback matters but continuous feedback is scarce
2. Limits of class observations, video recordings and generic PD
3. Technology for discourse-focused PD; building on ClassInSight; research questions
4. Study context, deployment and findings
5. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Need for feedback
- classroom constantly changing; course content + best-practice standards evolve
- adapt to individual students and group dynamics; plan lessons, reflect on practice, strategies to engage students
- feedback critical: what works, opportunities for positive change; reflective practices -> improved learning, more equitable participation
- continuous feedback hard to come by

2. Current options and limits
- class observations: expert in teacher training observes one or two class periods -> personalized, in-depth feedback
- review of studies: immediate feedback most effective for specific, corrective changes to teaching behaviors
- but observations focus on performance evaluation as employee, not personal growth
- subtle moves (conversational dynamics in discussions) hard for single observer in real-time
- expert observations more frequent for pre-service, less for in-service teachers (who would also benefit)
- video recordings: more accurate recollection, rich reflection opportunities; but great effort: setting up/testing equipment, curating actions worth reflecting on
- generic professional development (PD), workshops/seminars: scale, background on content/standards; no personalized, persistent guidance
- PD sessions mostly singular, no progress follow-ups; focus on standards/content, not individual goals, strategies, strengths

3. Technology for PD
- learning scientists: technology for observing teaching as personalized PD, esp. discourse pedagogy
- class discussion gives voice to students' reasoning, insight into student cognition and learning process
- low cost recording equipment can capture/model conversational dynamics
- several systems (research + commercial) use class audio for automated feedback on discussion practices
- open questions: design and impact in practice; relevant to HCI and educational technology communities
- we build on ClassInSight: visualizes classroom discussion data for personalized PD + conversation support
- approach: discourse visualizations + collaborative reflection with a PD researcher
- RQs: How did teachers use features of ClassInSight in reflections over time? What are the factors and barriers of adoption of discourse visualization tools?

4. Study
- collaborative design-based research (DBR) project, three research institutions
- middle and high school science teaching; guided reflection sessions with PD researcher
- expansion of Gomoll et al; three levels: Talk Ratio, Turn-Taking, Transcript (Figure 1); schema for noticings and reflections
- longitudinal deployment, 3 academic years, 5 middle/high school science teachers, large US city, 22 reflection sessions
- end-of-deployment interviews about experiences with prototype
- themes: quantification, contextualization, shifting professional vision, adoptability
- extends previous results: how interactions with data impact reflections over time

5. Contributions
- analysis of how design of ClassInSight (data-driven discussion analysis tool) impacts professional learning and reflection in teaching
- design implications for adoption of conversational support tools in professions lacking frequent personalized feedback (clinicians, vets, mentors, therapists, trainers, police, advisors, lawyers, consultants)
- lessons learned within and beyond teaching

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The classroom is an environment that is always changing. Course content changes, and the standards for best practices in teaching also keep evolving. Teachers have to adapt to the needs of individual students and at the same time to the group dynamics that make every class unique. They need to plan lessons, reflect on how effective their practices are, and come up with strategies to engage students. Feedback is critical for understanding what is working and for finding opportunities for positive change. Feedback can help teachers develop reflective practices that lead to improved student learning and more equitable participation. Unfortunately, it is hard for teachers to get continuous feedback.

In class observations, a professional with expertise in teacher training observes one or two class periods, and this can give teachers personalized, in-depth feedback about their teaching practices. A review of studies found that this kind of immediate feedback was most effective for specific and corrective changes to teaching behaviors. But observations often focus on evaluating the performance of the teacher as an employee and not on personal growth. Also, more subtle teaching moves, like conversational dynamics during class discussions, are hard for a single observer to make sense of in real-time. Expert teaching observations happen more often for pre-service teachers, but they are less common for in-service teachers, who would also benefit from continuous feedback. Video recordings are another option. They give a more accurate recollection of events and rich opportunities for reflection, but they take a lot of effort, for example setting up and testing the recording equipment and curating the actions in the recordings that are worth reflecting on. More generic forms of professional development (PD), like workshops and seminars, can scale and can give background on changing content and teaching standards, but they can't give the personalized and persistent guidance that is needed for effective change. Also, most teacher PD sessions happen only once and there is no opportunity to follow up on progress with new techniques and approaches. And PD mostly focuses on standards or content and not on individual goals, strategies and strengths.

Recently, learning scientists have looked at technology for observing teaching practices as a new type of personalized PD, especially for discourse pedagogy. Class discussion can give voice to students' reasoning and help teachers understand student cognition and the learning process better. Prior work found that even low cost recording equipment could accurately capture and model the conversational dynamics in the classroom. Several current systems, both research and commercial ones, use audio recordings of classes to give teachers automated feedback about their discussion practices. There are still open questions about how such tools should be designed and what impact they have in practice, and these questions matter to the HCI and educational technology communities for bridging research and practice. In our work we build on ClassInSight, a tool that visualizes classroom discussion data for personalized teacher PD and conversation support. Our approach to designing ClassInSight combines data visualizations of discourse with collaborative reflection with a PD researcher, and we want to answer the following research questions:

- • How did teachers use features of ClassInSight in reflections over time?

- • What are the factors and barriers of adoption of discourse visualization tools?

This is part of a collaborative design-based research (DBR) project among three research institutions. We situate ClassInSight in middle and high school science teaching and in guided reflection sessions where teachers discuss their class discussion data with a PD researcher. The tool is an expansion of Gomoll et al, and it visualizes classroom discussion data at three different levels: the Talk Ratio, Turn-Taking, and Transcript (Figure 1). Besides these visualizations, teachers also follow a schema to structure their noticings and reflections. In a longitudinal deployment over 3 academic years, 5 middle and high school science teachers from a large city in the United States took part in 22 reflection sessions where they engaged with their discussion data in the tool. When the deployment ended we interviewed the teachers to understand their experiences with using the prototype. From their interactions with the tool in the reflection sessions and from the interviews, we found themes about quantification, contextualization, shifting professional vision, and adoptability. We extend previous results by showing how interacting with data in ClassInSight impacts reflections over time.

We make the following contributions. First, we analyze how the design of ClassInSight, a data-driven discussion analysis tool, impacts professional learning and reflection in teaching. Second, we give design implications that influence whether conversational support tools get adopted in professions that also often lack frequent personalized feedback on professional interactions (e.g. clinicians, vets, mentors, therapists, trainers, police, advisors, lawyers, consultants). Our findings from deploying ClassInSight give lessons learned both within teaching and beyond it.

Learning scientists have recently investigated technology for observing teaching practices as a novel type of personalized PD, particularly for discourse pedagogy. Class discussion can give voice to students' reasoning and give teachers a greater understanding of student cognition and the learning process [19,20,21,22].
